flashcards.q: What are the perceptual latency thresholds for a voice agent, and where do they come from?
flashcards.a: Human turn-taking gaps average ~200 ms, so replies under ~800 ms feel natural/responsive; past ~800 ms pauses become consciously noticeable; past ~1500 ms the conversation feels broken (users repeat themselves or hang up). The thresholds derive from human conversation rhythm, not vendor marketing.

flashcards.q: Decompose the cascaded voice-agent round-trip budget stage by stage.
flashcards.a: Uplink+jitter buffer 50-100ms; endpointing 100-500ms; streaming STT partial <250ms; LLM time-to-first-token 100-600ms; TTS time-to-first-audio 90-313ms; plus 50-200ms inter-vendor network hops. Sequential sum ≈1400ms; streamed/overlapped ≈500-700ms.

flashcards.q: Why does overlapping stages matter more than raw component speed?
flashcards.a: A naive sequential pipeline costs ~1400ms; streaming every stage (STT partials feeding the LLM, sentence chunks feeding TTS while generation continues) overlaps them so only the critical path counts, landing at 500-700ms. Overlap is what crosses the felt-realtime line, not faster individual components.

flashcards.q: VAD vs endpointing — what different questions do they answer?
flashcards.a: VAD classifies individual short audio frames (~20-30ms) as speech/non-speech ('is there a voice right now?'); endpointing decides whether the whole turn has ended ('should the agent respond?'). VAD is one input to the endpointing decision, alongside transcript finality and semantics.

flashcards.q: Name the three VAD generations and their tradeoffs.
flashcards.a: Energy thresholding: free, fails in any realistic noise (documented in G.729-era work, 1997). GMM-based spectral (WebRTC VAD): tiny pure-C footprint, battle-tested, weak on babble/music/non-stationary noise. Neural (Silero, MIT, trained across 6,000+ languages, ONNX-deployable): robust at low SNR, modest compute cost.

flashcards.q: Why can't a single silence threshold solve endpointing?
flashcards.a: Silence duration contains no information distinguishing a hesitation from a completed thought — both look identical acoustically. Raising the threshold trades premature interruptions for dead air on every turn (400→800ms adds half a second per reply); lowering it cuts users off. Only semantic content separates them, hence semantic endpointing.

flashcards.q: What is semantic VAD / semantic endpointing?
flashcards.a: Scoring whether an utterance is meaningfully complete using lexical content, syntax, intonation, and fillers rather than silence duration alone. OpenAI's Realtime API exposes it as semantic_vad with an eagerness setting (low/medium/high/auto); dedicated turn-detection models (LiveKit turn detector, Deepgram Flux <300ms median EOT) make the respond-or-wait decision.

flashcards.q: Describe the barge-in mechanical loop and its deadline.
flashcards.a: On user speech during agent playback: detect via input-channel VAD → stop agent audio within ~150ms → flush TTS buffer and queued audio → cancel in-flight LLM generation → reroute incoming audio to STT. Requires acoustic echo cancellation so the agent doesn't hear its own TTS and interrupt itself.

flashcards.q: Why is 'first token' the LLM metric that matters in voice?
flashcards.a: Nothing downstream (chunking, TTS) can start until the first token arrives, so time-to-first-token is the LLM's entire contribution to perceived responsiveness; total generation hides under playback. Levers: fast model tier (100-200 vs 250-600ms TTFT), prompt caching, regional colocation, async tools with spoken filler.

flashcards.q: How should TTS text be chunked for streaming synthesis, and what breaks if done wrong?
flashcards.a: Chunk at punctuation/sentence boundaries: big enough for prosody, small enough for low time-to-first-audio. Too-small chunks cause mid-phoneme glitches on fragmentary words; too-large chunks inflate TTFA directly. Client keeps a ~200-300ms jitter buffer for network variance.

flashcards.q: Give representative 2026 TTS time-to-first-audio medians and why the spread matters.
flashcards.a: Gradium ~155ms, Cartesia Sonic-3 ~188ms, ElevenLabs Turbo v2.5 ~264ms (tight ~28ms IQR), ElevenLabs Flash v2.5 ~288ms, Deepgram Aura-2 ~313ms. The fastest-to-slowest spread exceeds 150ms — an entire barge-in budget — so engine choice materially moves the round trip.

Cascaded (STT→LLM→TTS): per-stage audit transcripts, your model choice, VPC-deployable, predictable $0.0095-$0.17/min. S2S (OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live): ~600-900ms end-to-end, native prosody/interruption, but transcript is derived/vendor-controlled, cost spread ~182x across providers. Enterprise defaults to cascaded unless feel is the product.

flashcards.q: Median response is 400ms but users say it feels slow — diagnosis?
flashcards.a: Percentile masking: p50 hides the tail, and subjective experience anchors on worst turns — average 400ms routinely coexists with p99 of 2.5s. Instrument per-stage p95/p99 (OTel spans), find the tail source (endpointing policy, cold connections, uncached prompts, TTS variance), alert on tails not means.

flashcards.q: Why do pre-roll and hangover exist in every real VAD wrapper?
flashcards.a: Pre-roll: the trigger always fires after speech started, so you keep ~200ms of audio before the trigger to avoid clipping word onsets. Hangover: trailing frames of tolerance (~400ms) so low-amplitude mid-speech isn't clipped — hysteresis converting a noisy frame-level signal into stable region decisions; heritage goes back to G.729's fifteen 10ms overhang frames.

flashcards.q: What belongs in a production voice-agent evaluation suite beyond LLM-judge answer checks?
flashcards.a: Per-stage metrics (ASR accuracy per accent/noise cohort, turn-error rate, TTFA p50/p95/p99), task completion, and audio-level naturalness (blind ELO scoring catches silent vendor model rotations). Run nightly synthetic-call regression (interruptions, noise, packet loss, code-switching) gating deploys in CI — transcript-level judging is blind to all voice-specific failures.
